state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's think about it this way: imagine you have a group of friends who all have different heights. If everyone in the group suddenly grew by the same amount, would the tallest and shortest friends stay the same? Think about how this might apply to the plants in Tom and Katie's discussion.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I think I get what you're saying. If everyone grows by the same amount, the tallest and shortest would still be the same, so the range would change. But I'm still not sure how that works with Tom's example of cutting the plants in half. Wouldn't the tallest and shortest still be the same proportionally?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's think of it this way: imagine you have a group of friends where each person's height is doubled. Would the tallest and shortest still be the same proportionally? Think about how this might relate to Tom's example of cutting the plants in half.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I think I see what you're saying, but I'm still a bit confused. If I double everyone's height, the tallest and shortest would still be the same proportionally, right? So, if Tom cuts the plants in half, wouldn't the range still change because the actual heights are different now? I'm not sure how that works.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher uses analogies to prompt reasoning but never directly addresses the proportional vs. additive distinction at the heart of the misconception, and the student remains confused throughout, showing no improvement and actually deepening their confusion by Turn 4.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses concrete real-world analogies (friends' heights, growing, doubling) to help the student understand the abstract mathematical concept of range, which is a textbook example of the experiential strategy.
